A library portal showed slow searches after a configuration rollout and during a backup. Write exactly three short paragraphs on the evidence, two competing explanations, and a read-only check. Finish with END OF HANDOFF.

Searches slowed after a configuration rollout while a backup was running. The record gives the order of events, and the overlap leaves both changes under consideration.

The rollout may have increased work per query. The backup may have increased storage contention. Either could affect search latency, and both could contribute at the same time.

Compare the query plan and database read latency before and during the slowdown. A changed plan supports the rollout hypothesis. Storage wait rising across unrelated queries supports backup contention.

END OF HANDOFF

In a tabletop, P1 says staging reviewers may approve only requests assigned to them. P2 is a screenshot of an approved sample with the reviewer ID hidden. P3 is an approval log for that record with no session ID. Use exactly four headings Scope, Evidence, Alternatives, Retest. Cite P1–P3 and give one measurable criterion. End with END OF TABLETOP.

## Scope
The assessment covers staging and sample records. P1 defines the expected approval boundary for reviewers assigned to a request.

## Evidence
P2 shows the sample approval with the reviewer ID hidden. P3 confirms that an approval event was recorded for the same record. The two artifacts leave the session and reviewer unidentified.

## Alternatives
An assigned reviewer could have made the approval through the intended workflow. A different reviewer could also have been permitted to approve it. Compare a correlated session record with the assignment at the time of the approval to distinguish these possibilities.

## Retest
With pre-issued staging accounts, record the expected decision for five assigned and five unassigned sample approvals. Require all five unassigned approvals to be denied and all five assigned approvals to succeed. Verify that each decision has a session and reviewer ID.

END OF TABLETOP

Write a handoff about a document search outage. Data: rollout at 13:00 UTC, latency rose at 13:04, background indexing started at 13:02, no confirmed cause. Use headings Timeline, Hypotheses, Checks, Recovery. Include one test per hypothesis and end with END HANDOFF.

## Timeline
At 13:00 UTC the rollout began. Background indexing began at 13:02. Search latency rose at 13:04. The cause remains under investigation.

## Hypotheses
The rollout may have increased query cost. Indexing may have competed with search for disk throughput.

## Checks
Compare read-only query plans for the same search from before and after the rollout. Compare indexer throughput with storage wait time and search latency during the same minutes. Higher storage wait across unchanged queries would support contention.

## Recovery
Before closing the incident, verify sustained search latency near the pre-rollout baseline and check that indexing progress continues. Record the measurement window and any mitigation so the next shift can verify the change.

END HANDOFF

Write a 300–400 word engineering handoff in four sections: Timeline, Competing Causes, Read-Only Investigation, and Recovery. At 07:40 UTC a search index rebuild began. At 07:48 a feature flag started sending 20% of queries to a new ranking path. Search p95 rose from 180 ms to 1.4 s at 07:51. Request volume was steady. Index workers and search run on shared storage. No per-route or storage metrics have been reviewed yet. Include a different read-only check for each cause, and end with END HANDOFF.

## Timeline
At 07:40 UTC the search index rebuild began on storage shared with search. At 07:48 the feature flag began sending 20% of queries through the new ranking path. Search p95 rose from 180 ms to 1.4 s at 07:51 while request volume remained steady. The overall p95 may hide a difference between routes, so the handoff should retain the times and traffic share when comparing the two paths.

## Competing Causes
The rebuild could increase storage contention, making otherwise similar queries slower on both ranking paths. Another possibility is that the new path costs more per query, which could raise the aggregate p95 even if the existing path stays healthy. Both effects could occur at once. Steady request volume helps rule out a simple volume spike as the sole explanation, while query mix and per-query work remain open questions.

## Read-Only Investigation
For the storage hypothesis, inspect historical storage queue depth and read latency around the rebuild start, flag change, and slowdown. Compare those series with request latency on the existing ranking route. A rise on that route with storage wait would support contention, especially if latency later tracks rebuild throughput. For the ranking hypothesis, break down p95, errors, and request counts by flag assignment and compare similar query types over the same time window. If the new route is slower than the existing route under similar storage conditions, inspect the corresponding sampled traces to see which stage accounts for the difference.

## Recovery
Assess recovery when both paths have stable latency near their pre-incident baselines on comparable traffic, with enough requests on each route to make the p95 meaningful. Record the observation window, flag share, and rebuild status in the handoff. Check that search results remain available and that the index rebuild is progressing or has completed. If only the aggregate improves, keep the incident open until the per-route measurements establish which users still see slow queries.

END HANDOFF

Write a 280–380 word incident review in four sections: Scope, Facts, Hypotheses, and Verification. A sandbox-only authorization exercise produced a synthetic export success at 10:08 UTC. The role matrix limits exporting to supervisors. The UI capture shows an export banner but the identity is cropped. The application event contains the export ID, and a separate identity log has two nearby sign-ins with no shared identifier. The alert arrived at 10:16. Include one control retest and one alerting retest with measurable outcomes. End with END OF EXERCISE.

## Scope
This review covers the sandbox exercise, synthetic records, and the authorization and alerting controls that were exercised. Treat the role matrix as the expected policy for the exercise. The scope also covers the evidence needed to tie an export to a known sandbox identity.

## Facts
The role matrix grants export permission to supervisors. The application recorded a successful synthetic export at 10:08 UTC and included an export ID. The UI capture shows an export banner, with the identity outside the visible frame. The identity log contains two nearby sign-ins. The records provided have no shared identifier that links either sign-in to the export. An alert arrived at 10:16 UTC, eight minutes after the recorded export. That interval measures observed delay and leaves the responsible stage of the alert pipeline unresolved.

## Hypotheses
An authorized supervisor could have performed the export while the other sign-in was unrelated. A lower-privilege test account could have exported the record if enforcement diverged from the matrix. Comparing sign-in times alone gives weak attribution because both sessions existed near the export. A staging request trace linking export ID, session ID, authenticated role at decision time, and policy outcome could distinguish the two explanations. The banner by itself only shows what the interface displayed.

## Verification
For the authorization retest, use registered sandbox accounts and five synthetic export attempts per role. Require five successful supervisor attempts and five denied lower-privilege attempts, with a role decision and export or request ID captured for every result. For the alerting retest, use five designated alert-triggering sandbox events. Require each alert to arrive within five minutes of the source event and include its request ID. Compare event, ingestion, detection, and notification timestamps for any miss so the team can locate the delay before closing the exercise.

END OF EXERCISE
